speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FINAL SETTLEMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL   ADDITION OF $65 MILLION TO SUMS AWAITING DISTRIBUTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a brief statement to make concerning the final settlement of the five-year wheat pool.

maintopic: FINAL SETTLEMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL   ADDITION OF $65 MILLION TO SUMS AWAITING DISTRIBUTION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FINAL SETTLEMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL   ADDITION OF $65 MILLION TO SUMS AWAITING DISTRIBUTION
speechtext:
Perhaps the applause might be deferred until I make the statement.
As the house is aware, there have been discussions with the United Kingdom government on several occasions concerning article 2(b) of the wheat agreement entered into in 1946-the so-called "have regard to" clause. The United Kingdom government has made it clear that no further payment will be made by them under that agreement. Hon. members may also have seen an announcement by the Chancellor of the Exchequer on February 20 that the United Kingdom will not draw further on the remainder of the credit of $1,250 million which was made available in May, 1946, and which expires on December 31, 1951.
The government has decided to recommend to parliament that an amount equal to the balance of the United Kingdom credit, namely, $65 million, be added to the sums now awaiting distribution in settlement of the five-year pool. The amount will be included in the final supplementary estimates for the fiscal year 1950-51 which are shortly to be placed before the house for approval.
The contribution we will be asking parliament to make is the equivalent of about 23 cents per bushel on the deliveries made during the last two years of the agreement to which article 2(b) had reference. The addition of $65 million to the pool would make a total of approximately $120 million for distribution. On the basis of deliveries of 1,428 million bushels during the period of the five-year pool, this would provide a final payment of about 8-3 cents per bushel. Final payments will be made as soon as possible after parliament has dealt with the supplementary estimates.	>

subtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 77, respecting the department of defence production.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: MOBILIZATION OF ECONOMIC AND INDUSTRIAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary to speak at length on this bill. The Prime Minister has already pointed out the need for a separate department to carry out the procurement functions needed for the defence program, and to control essential materials to meet these requirements.
The bill before the house is designed to do three things. In the first place, it will establish a department of defence production. Second, it would confer powers on the minister with respect to procurement very similar to those formerly held by the minister of munitions and supply. Third, it would confer powers on the governor in council and on the minister to control essential materials in substantially the same terms as the present Essential Materials (Defence) Act.
It is proposed that the act would expire on July 31, 1956. There is no particular significance to this date, other than to recognize that some of the powers sought in this bill are special powers which should not be of a continuing nature. Bearing in mind the present situation, and the program which has been announced by my colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), a period of five years seems a reasonable minimum for the duration of the act. In the bill, provision is also made for the repeal of the Essential Materials (Defence) Act and for the suspension of the Defence Supplies Act during the period of operation of the Defence Production Act.
The more detailed proposals under each of the three heads that I have mentioned are as follows:
Departmental organization and responsibility.-There are the usual provisions for a minister and a deputy minister. Departmental staff is to be employed as far as possible under the normal procedures of the Civil Service Act, although the minister with the approval of the governor in council is to be given special authority to engage personnel outside the normal procedure. The temporary nature of the act, and the special nature of the staff to be recruited, make this course advisable. Because of the specialized nature of much of the work to be done by the new department it is expected the staff
[Mr. Garson.l

will need many skills and abilities not normally available to the public service. Since the act will be temporary, these employees will not come under the Superannuation Act, but arrangements are being made to protect existing contributors.
The bill also provides that crown companies may be set up to assist the minister in the administration of the act. The efficiency of this technique of operation needs little explanation to anyone who has had experience with it during the last war. The bill provides that the minister may authorize departmental staff to act on his behalf and he may employ companies to act as agents of the crown. There are the usual provisions relating to actions against crown companies.
The responsibilities of the minister include the administration of the act, the exclusive procurement of defence supplies, and the construction of defence projects for the Department of National Defence. In addition, the minister is to be responsible for Canadian Arsenals Limited, Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, Defence Construction Limited, Polymer Corporation Limited, Jdorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited and its subsidiary, Northern Transportation Company (1947) Limited, and Canadian Commeicial Corporation. Provision is made to transfer the administration in relation to these matters from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In connection with defence procurement, the bill igives the minister powers to undertake the organization of industry for defence purposes. In this connection, he will be authorized to require returns from persons who have defence supplies or the facilities to produce them, and from those constructing defence projects or having facilities for storage.
Procurement and production.-The powers proposed to be conferred on the minister for procurement include acquiring, holding and disposing of defence supplies; manufacturing or producing them; or operating facilities for these purposes. The powers also cover the construction and maintenance of defence projects, and permit the minister to employ commercial services and acquire property for these purposes. The bill also provides for authority to make loans or advances to assist in carrying out these functions.
It is also proposed that there should be a defence production revolving fund of $100 million for the following three purposes: (a) to finance stockpiling of defence supplies which include strategic materials; (b) to make loans or advances to aid in defence procurement, for example, working capital loans or advance payments on contracts, but not including advance for capital purpose; (c) to

permit the department to make initial payments for defence supplies, which will be subsequently reimbursed by the Department of National Defence. While there was no provision for a revolving fund in the Munitions and Supply Act, the procedure was actually followed during the last war under the War Measures Act and the War Appropriation Act. It was found to be the only practicable method of dealing with many of the situations that arose.
The provisions requiring prior approval by the governor in council of contracts entered into by the minister are substantially those now contained in the Defence Supplies Act.
In relation to defence contracts, the minister would have powers (a) to direct that they be performed in priority to the contractors' other work or within a fixed period, as is now provided under the Defence Supplies Act; (b) to renegotiate in a similar way to that provided under the Department of Munitions and Supply Act with an appeal to the exchequer court-this will not apply to contracts entered into before the act comes into force; (c) to direct an investigation into the performance of defence contracts; and (d) to appoint a controller to operate a person's business if he is not carrying out a defence contract properly or if he fails to keep proper books or accounts.
The minister would also have power to direct a person, for fair and reasonable compensation, to store defence supplies or to undertake production. The minister could also requisition defence supplies necessary for defence purposes in return for reasonable compensation in much the same way as is now provided under the Defence Supplies Act. In each case, provision is made for an appeal to the exchequer court.
Control of essential markets.-In connection with essential materials, the powers to be conferred are identical with those under the Essential Materials (Defence) Act. The plan is that the governor in council may designate "materials or substances" which are considered necessary to control ini order to ensure availability of defence supplies. The governor in council may make regulations, and the minister has wide powers of control, in relation to materials so designated.
It is under these powers of the Essential Materials (Defence) Act that the steel limitation orders have been issued. Similarly, although formal orders have not been issued in the field of non-ferrous metals, the producers of the five principal metals are now operating a plan of rationing whereby deliveries to their customers are regulated. In the case of nickel each customer may be supplied
Defence Production Act with primary metal on the basis of 65 per cent of his average monthly purchases during 1950. In the cases of copper, zinc, aluminum and lead the basis is 100 per cent of his average monthly purchases during 1950.
One important addition that is made to previous powers, and that runs throughout the whole bill, is provision for powers of procurement and of regulation of essential materials to be used by the minister for the benefit of associated governments; that is, for member nations of the commonwealth, North Atlantic treaty nations, and for nations whose defence the governor in council considers vital to Canada.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has already mentioned, I have, at his request, supervised the drafting of this bill, and I have also given a good deal of thought to the type of organization that will be needed to deal with matters pertaining to defence production and supply. In the Department of Trade and Commerce we have, in the last few months, been attempting to lay the foundation for an organization to carry out these functions. The steps taken so far have been under the authority of the Essential Materials (Defence) Act and the Defence Supplies Act. These have included the establishment of separate units within the Department of Trade and Commerce to deal with steel, base metals, explosives and chemicals, priorities and finance, and the setting up of a crown company to deal with defence construction. Arrangements will be made to have all of these come under the direction of the Minister of Defence Production.
Present plans being suggested for the new department provide for the setting up of three main operating branches, together with a number of auxiliary branches to service the main branches and the department as a whole.
First of all, there would be a branch concerned with the major production programs. In this branch there would be divisions, or where necessary, crown companies, to deal with the production of vehicles, ammunition, guns and armament, et cetera, and in such fields as aircraft, shipbuilding, construction and electronics. I announced February 28 that we had been successful in securing the services of Crawford Gordon, Jr., of Toronto, to act as co-ordinator of this branch. Some months ago I announced the appointment of R. G. Johnson to direct the construction program through the facilities of a crown company, Defence Construction Limited, of which he is president. I can now announce the appointments of J. M. Cochrane of Windsor, Ontario, to direct the vehicle program; E. Barker of Toronto to direct the machine tool

Defence Production Act division; and H. R. Malley, president of Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, to direct the gun and ammunition division. Other appointments will be announced as made for such programs as aircraft, shipbuilding, electronics, and any other divisions that it may be found necessary to establish.
The second main branch of the department would concern itself with materials needed to carry out the defence program. A number of the divisions which would form this branch have, as I have said already, been established in the Department of Trade and Commerce. We have a steel division under the direction of Kenneth S. Harris; a nonferrous metals division under the direction of F. V. C. Hewett; a chemicals division under the direction of J. R. Donald, who served in the same capacity in the Department of Munitions and Supply during the last war; a petroleum division under the direction of Dr. Oliver Hopkins; and a priorities division under the direction of Henry J. Sissons. These five divisions are already in operation, or are in the process of formation, and would be transferred to the new department. Others would be established as circumstances dictate.
The third main branch of the new department would be the general purchasing branch, which would consist of the central organization of the Canadian Commercial Corporation. The Canadian Commercial Corporation now acts as an agent of the minister in carrying out procurement of the requirements of the three services. With a separate department of defence production, the general purchasing would be carried out as a direct function of the department and the great majority of the staff of the Canadian Commercial Corporation would be transferred to the department for that purpose. This branch would be responsible for the procurement of all items that were not the direct responsibility of the production or materials branches that I have described. It is not proposed, however, to wind up the corporation as such, but rather to retain it as a special agency to handle transactions with other governments or to engage in the bulk purchasing or stockpiling of any defence supplies or strategic materials that may be necessary. The corporation, with such terms of reference, would probably fulfil a role not dissimilar to that filled by War Supplies Limited during the last war.
In addition to these three main branches, there would be a financial adviser, who, with his staff, would be concerned with the general financial policy of the department, involving such matters as capital assistance, accelerated depreciation and problems of renegotiation and profit limitation. I was pleased to be

able to announce the other day that the government had been successful in securing the services of Mr. Harold G. Hesler, of Montreal, to fill this important post.
Then there would, of course, have to be a legal branch, an administration branch, a controller's branch, and an economics and statistics branch, as well as a branch dealing with the various types of international relations with which the department would be concerned. The latter involves arrangements with NATO, problems relating to the allocation and distribution of assistance made available to our North Atlantic treaty allies, and general questions in the international field such as the allocation of raw materials on an international basis.
In the development of the program thus far, and in laying plans for the future, I have been greatly assisted by numerous individuals in the business community who have been most generous in the giving of their time and advice. In addition, I would like to mention specifically the help that has been rendered by two organizations.
The first is the industrial defence board originally set up by my colleague, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), and subsequently transferred under my jurisdiction. Under the able chairmanship of Mr. H. J. Carmichael, who so successfully filled the role in the last war of co-ordinator of production, this board has rendered valuable service in examining various proposals from industry and in making recommendations. Most of the members of that board will be associated with the defence production program in some direct capacity. With the proposal to establish a separate department of defence production, it therefore seems unnecessary to continue the industrial defence board as such. The board was established just three years ago and as its members were appointed for a three-year term, it is proposed that the board should wind up its activities and disband within the next month or so. I should like at this time to extend the thanks of the government to the members of this board for the excellent service that they have .rendered.
The other agency to which I wish to refer is the Canadian Industrial Preparedness Association. This organization was established several years ago on a voluntary basis by a number of manufacturers who felt that, in the event of another emergency, they would be directly involved in the production of war supplies. The organization, which consists of a number of individual industry groups, has concerned itself with the steps that private industry could take to prepare for just such a period as we are now entering, which calls for greatly expanded defence

production. Much valuable work has been done by the organization, but I might mention specifically the service that they rendered in connection with the visits to Canada of the various task forces of the North Atlantic treaty organization. These task forces were concerned with developing information on the productive capabilities of the various members of the North Atlantic treaty. The association took the responsibility for reception of these visitors to Canada, and organized their inspection of the various plants in which they were interested. This association is not government sponsored, but we welcome its existence and look forward to a very close association with it in the future.
In introducing this bill at this time, the government is carrying out plans for war mobilization that it has been developing over the past few years. The experience in the last war showed the wisdom of building a separate department for defence production. Since the end of the last war, the nucleus of such a department has been retained. What is now proposed is to expand this nucleus to meet the increasing demands upon it and to establish a special department of government which should be vested with wide powers. Some of these powers are ones that are appropriate at any time, whether in peace, in war, or in the present state of international tension. By and large, these are the powers that are now contained in the Defence Supplies Act, which, hon. members will notice, is only being suspended during the life of the present proposed act. Other powers are of an extraordinary nature but fitted to the extraordinary circumstances of today.
There will be little disagreement in any part of the house that speed in getting on with the defence preparations is of the utmost importance. This need for speed dictates the need for special powers both to requisition supplies and to direct production, as well as special authority to renegotiate contracts. The government makes no apology for asking for these extensive powers at this time, and the record of its administration of similar powers which it exercised during the last war speaks for itself.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the principle of this bill, as members of the official opposition see it, is to set up a department of defence production, whose main aim will be the purchasing of defence supplies for Canada and for her allies. Because we believe that to be the main principle of the bill we propose to support it. However, we do ask that the
Defence Production Act members of the government, and the members of the house, give further consideration to some of the terms which are set out in this bill. The minister himself described them accurately in the last moment of his speech when he said they were extraordinary powers.
In addition to setting up a department, this bill interferes drastically with the rights of the individual Canadian, and also overrides parliament to a degree which we believe unnecessary and unwise at this time-in fact, to a degree which is justifiable only when the nation is in the midst of war; and even under those conditions the wisdom of using some of those powers is very questionable.
In fact, this bill gives the minister full wartime powers. It is a war bill. It gives him all the powers that would be required if we were in a third world war. But that is not the position. The country is not in a third world war. The policy of Canada, and also the policy of the other free nations, is to become strong quickly and thus prevent war, and to continue strong in the hope that eventually Russia will decide that cooperation is the best policy.
I read in some of the journals that the Americans expect to reach the apex of their strength within the next year or two, and that then they will level off at that strength. In other words it is their intention to continue strong. The position here in Canada was very clearly outlined by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself when he spoke to the Liberal federation in this city earlier this week, upon which occasion he said:
Today we are trying to prevent world war III. That, too, is going to require a tremendous effort: but it is going to be different in many ways from what we were doing ten or eleven years ago. Some of the things we did then have to be done again. But other things called' for to win a shooting war are completely unsuited to the task of preventing a shooting war.
As we see it, this policy adopted by Canada, and agreed to by all members in the house, is a long-term policy. If it succeeds it will prevent war; but we must all admit that it is bound to be a long-term policy. Canada is in for a long pull; this is no short-term plan that we have adopted. That fact must be kept in mind when considering a bill of this kind, and particularly the wartime powers given under the bill.
As the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) explained quite frankly today, the powers in the bill are derived largely from the old Department of Munitions and Supply Act, which was passed in 1939 after the outbreak of war, was amended in 1940 to give additional powers, and was further
840	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act amended in 1943 to give further powers, with the result that as finally amended it gave the then minister of munitions and supply, who is now Minister of Trade and Commerce, the widest possible powers that could be written in the English language.
The minister himself explained that very clearly last June when he was speaking in the debate on the Defence Supplies Act. I would refer hon. members to page 3489 of Hansard for June 12, 1950, where he said:
The Munitions and Supply Act was wartime legislation which gave the minister the widest possible powers; power to renegotiate contracts, power to order a man to accept a contract at prices fixed by the minister, and various other arbitrary powers.
All those powers, and more, are included in the bill now before us. It contains the provisions of an act known as the Essential Materials (Defence) Act, which was passed at the special session last fall. In the debate on that bill the minister made a statement as to the powers he was taking. It appears at page 448 of Hansard for that special session, at which point, referring to the Essential Materials (Defence) Act he said:
We believe that, barring a major emergency, the powers of the act will be sufficient to cope with the problem we anticipate.
That was last September. In addition to the powers contained in the two acts to which I have just referred, there are here also additional powers, such as the setting up of a revolving fund of $100 million, and various other provisions.
I propose to outline some of these powers the need for which at this time we question. They are powers which interfere with the rights of the individual Canadian, and we believe sincerely that they should be considered again by the government and the house before they are put in statute form.
The first is the power to force a person to enter into a contract. Whether he wants to contract or not, under the provisions of section 23 of the bill he can be compelled to do so. That is the power to which the minister referred last June when he mentioned a power "to order a man to accept a contract at prices fixed by the minister". It should be remembered too that practically all of these powers are exercised, not by the cabinet but by the minister, and also by anyone the minister may wish to appoint.
Then there is the power to take over that man's business, if he does not comply with the direction to enter into a contract with the government. The minister or his appointee can take over that man's business in whole or in part and appoint a controller to run the


business, including that portion which has nothing whatever to do with a defence contract. There is a further provision in the bill that such controller will be under no legal liability if he exceeds his authority.
That is a pretty drastic power to be approved by parliament, if indeed we intend to retain here any powers at all. The power to take over a business is found in section 27, and the same section includes power to take over in whole or in part the business of a Canadian who has already entered into a contract. I am now referring to the man who has actually made a contract; the man about whom I spoke a few moments ago was the one who did not contract and was forced by the government to do business with it.
With regard to both of these men we find that if the minister or his appointee thinks that a man is likely to fail to carry out a contract, the business can be taken over. It is not the power of taking it over only if there is failure under the contract, but also of taking it over if the minister or his appointee is satisfied that there will be failure, or that there is likely to be. That decision, whether it is thought that a Canadian is likely to fail, is left entirely in the hands of the minister or the minister's appointee. There may be one appointee to decide with regard to one class of business, another appointee to decide with respect to another class of business and so on.
There is also the very wide power contained in the bill to conduct an investigation into the business of a Canadian. It is contained in section 29. The minister or an appointee of the minister can order an investigator to walk into anybody's business to investigate all the details thereof. Provision is made that if the investigator exceeds his authority he is not liable. He is under no obligation. The businessman who has had his business investigated, and has been caused damage or loss because the investigator has gone too far, has no remedy. That is under the provisions of section 36 of the bill, the same section which exempts a controller who exceeds his authority from any liability.
Then there is a provision that, if the minister or the minister's appointee so directs, a businessman is freed from any obligations which may be imposed upon him by a contract that he has made with someone else, by bylaw of a municipality or by a statute either of this parliament or a provincial legislature. In section 28 there is the power to brush aside municipal bylaws, and laws of this parliament and of provincial legislatures.
There is also the power to which I have been referring which gives the minister the

right to assign all his powers. That is found in section 5, which reads:
The minister may authorize any person, on his behalf and under his control and direction, to do any act or thing or to exercise any power that the minister may do or exercise under this act.
Those are only some of the extraordinary powers contained in the bill which we believe should be considered further before they become law. There are some powers in the bill which we approve. For example, there are powers taken to prevent profiteering. We believe that such powers are properly placed in the bill because no one in a responsible position in Canada today wants any profiteering under present conditions, or for that matter under any other conditions.
There is also in the bill a very strong penalty section setting out the penalties for offences. That is quite a proper provision and we suggest under present conditions the minister should depend on these penalty sections rather than these powers to take over a man's business and all the other extraordinary powers contained in the bill. If a businessman commits an offence under the act, then let him be brought into court where he will get a fair hearing, where he will have a chance to be defended and to have his case properly considered; in that way people will have some rights and not be subject to a touch on the shoulder by somebody appointed by the assistant assistant deputy minister, or something of that kind.
You see, Mr. Speaker, the bill is out of line with the Emergency Powers Act which received third reading a few moments ago. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was careful to point out that he did not want to use the War Measures Act under present conditions. He said this was not the proper time to use that act. He said: We are not in a state of war and we are not in what could be considered a state of apprehended war. Therefore I am proposing to use a special act known as the Emergency Powers Act, not as strong a measure as the War Measures Act. He believed that such a policy was in line with the present times, and we are asking that this bill be of the same type as the Emergency Powers Act; in other words, an act in line with the times. The government cannot have it both ways. If it is wrong to use the War Measures Act under present conditions then it is wrong to use this particular measure. There should be the same kind of act to meet these two different problems.
We are suggesting that the government delete these powers from the bill. In his speech today the minister demonstrated no need for such powers. He did not bother to
Defence Production Act outline any need for the extraordinary powers to which I have referred. He simply said: They are in the bill and there they are going to stay. There was no attempt to justify putting these extraordinary powers into the act.
If the situation deteriorates, if the possibility of war becomes greater, if tension increases, then the house can very quickly amend this act and grant further powers. That was done in 1940. The original Munitions and Supply Department Act was passed at the special session called when war first broke out. It was not proclaimed for many months afterwards. When we met in 1940 for our regular session further powers were given. If the house is not sitting at the time the situation grows worse then the government can take further powers under the provisions of the Emergency Powers Act passed a few moments ago. Let us not make these extraordinary powers part of the peacetime statute law of Canada. It is far better to exercise them by order in council under the Emergency Powers Act than to make them a part of the permanent law.
If the government will not agree to that suggestion, if these extraordinary powers must remain in the bill, then let there be some distinction made in the measure between extraordinary powers and the powers to which there can be no objection. That could be done by providing that those sections of the act containing the objectionable powers would be brought into effect only by proclamation. Let them not come into effect when the bill comes into operation, but insert a provision that they can be brought in later by proclamation.
So much for the powers interfering unduly with the rights of the individual. Finally let me deal with the manner in which this bill overrides parliament. There is no provision in the bill requiring this department to file an annual report. In 1949 three new departments were set up, and each of the acts contained this provision with regard to an annual report:
The minister shall submit to parliament within thirty days of the commencement of the first session of parliament in each year a report showing the operations of the department during the year then last preceding.
I do urge that this bill be amended to provide for the filing of an annual report. Such a provision was also contained in the legislation setting up the department of reconstruction.

I think it will help preserve the rights of parliament if provision is made for an annual report. Then there is no provision whatever in this bill for the tabling of orders in council and regulations enacted under its provisions. I would point out that in the legislation setting up the department of reconstruction, which was chapter 18 of the statutes of 1944, provision was made for the tabling of orders and regulations. That provision is in section 9, dealing with the orders and regulations which were to help carryout the terms of the bill. It reads:
Orders and regulations under this section shall forthwith be published in the Canada Gazette and laid before parliament within fifteen days after they are made if parliament is then sitting, and, if not, then within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof.
A similar provision was contained in the Essential Materials (Defence) Act which was passed at the special session last fall. That is also section 9, which reads:
Every order or regulation made by the governor in council under sections three, four or ten shall be published forthwith in the Canada Gazette and shall be laid before parliament within ten days after publication thereof, if parliament is then in session, or, if parliament is not then in session, within ten days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof.
So I urge the minister that a similar section be written into this bill providing that these orders in council and regulations be tabled in the House of Commons.
With regard to the time limit, the minister has pointed out that the period provided in the bill is five years; in other words it is continued in effect until 1956. The defence plan outlined a few days ago by the Minister of National Defence covered a period of three years. The Essential Materials (Defence) Act passed during the special session of 1950 was to be in effect for a period of two years. The munitions and supply act passed in 1939 was for a period of three years. Subsequently that time limit was extended but in the original act there was a definite time limit of three years.
Yesterday in the other place-and the minister's parliamentary assistant will correct me if I am wrong-I believe an amendment was made to the Export and Import Permits Act; the provision in the bill as introduced, providing that it would be in effect for five years, was changed by those in the other place to three years. So I urge the minister to agree to cut the length of time during which this legislation will be in existence from five


years to three years-. That would give parliament just that much more opportunity to keep some control over the legislation and over the new department. No harm can be done by making the time limit three years instead of five, and I believe it would be much better if such a change were made.
Then this afternoon the minister made some explanation of the new type of financing provided i>n this bill which includes provision for a revolving fund and also, by the way, for the operation of several crown companies and the right to set up more. We all know how difficult it has always been for parliament to make a proper check of expenditures by these crown corporations. I believe that it will also be very difficult to keep track of the expenditures made under this revolving fund. When the bill gets into committee I hope there will be a full discussion of this question of financing the new department, because we are not yet satisfied that the proposed- system is the proper one.
In conclusion, many of the rights of the individual Canadian and of parliament were given up during the last war, and quite properly so. Those rights have -not yet been fully restored. The policy now is to prevent war; yet we find that these same powers are being taken again, not just for the duration of a war but for an indefinite term, perhaps for five years, perhaps for ten years, perhaps for twenty-five years. We are afraid that if this period should be very long the Canadian people will forget that they ever had these rights. There are young Canadians coming along, and the first thing we know we will have a generation with no knowledge of any system other than giving the government all these rights. That is bound to mean a decrease in the strength and independence of the individual. The same is true of parliament. It will mean a decrease in the strength of the nation.
We do urge upon the minister, and his associates in the government, that they give further consideration to these extraordinary powers contained in this bill, and that they allow time for the private members in the house to give further consideration to those changes. I believe that if that is done we shall be able to work out a bill which will more nearly fit the situation today than the bill under consideration.

I noticed that the minister said this bill had no political significance. This group would disagree with the minister to some extent in that respect. All parties in this house, Mr. Speaker, have expressed support of the principle of this bill. They realize the necessity for the establishment of a department of defence production. Without a doubt this is a most important bill, much more important possibly than many of the Canadian people realize at the moment. It will have a great effect on the economy of this country, and upon the personal lives of the Canadian people. There is no question about that. This group, Mr. Speaker, considers that the defence effort-when I say "this group" I mean the C.C.F. group-is a defence of freedom, and a defence of future opportunities to expand the frontiers of political and economic democracy.
I would judge, Mr. Speaker, after reading the bill that the government considers our defence effort is an effort to maintain capitalist democracy. I believe that is an accurate statement. Evidence of that is found, Mr. Speaker, in its recognition even in this defence effort of the profit incentive, regardless of the pressure of the emergency or whether this is termed a struggle for survival. No matter how great the emergency or the nation's need, even in building a defence effort under today's emergency conditions, without question the government is forced to give some consideration to the profit incentive. I believe it is further evidenced, Mr. Speaker, in the government's failure to interfere in what are considered the normal workings of this capitalist system by the establishment of the controls for which the members of this house have been asking in previous debates, and which would protect the living standards of the Canadian people. It is evidenced in the refusal to establish a rate of taxation that will make it impossible for anyone to gain an advantage from the nation's distress, and the refusal to make sufficient provision for the housing of many Canadians without housing today.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, there are two angles to our defence production program. There is the political angle, which has significance, and the economic angle. I think there is no question about it, the minister's ability as an administrator is recognized from the 80709-54 i

When you can read in the bill a clause which indicates that the minister is equal to His Majesty the King-I never read that in a bill before-the minister is without a doubt assuming immense powers. Our criticism of the minister and his colleagues under present conditions is that they lack a social awareness and understanding of the Canadian people's hopes and aspirations. In our opinion freedom can only be defended and maintained, Mr. Speaker, by the co-operation of freedom-loving people. When we come to the question of a defence production program, not only are there economic aspects of the program but there are political aspects, and the political aspects have to do with the question of morale. Morale depends, first of all, on the faith of the people in the democratic way of life, and also in this government continuing to give effect to progressive democratic policies.
Without question, production under our defence program depends to a great extent on morale. In the House of Commons on February 1 of this year the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said, as reported at page 27 of Hansard:
What we shall be asking parliament to authorize will not be aid or assistance to anybody else. It will be something required by ourselves for the purpose of doing our part in building up this joint strength which is required to fulfil an undertaking that no one of us alone could fulfil and one that can be fulfilled only by the full co-operative efforts of all of us.
Then quoting from the Ottawa Citizen of March 1, under the heading "Inflation to cut Standards", I note that, when the Prime Minister was speaking at the annual banquet of the advisory council of the national Liberal federation, he is reported as saying:

To date in the debate on the minister's announcement with regard to our defence program, in the debate on the emergency bill, and in the debate on this bill, ministers and others have emphasized the fact that this is a national emergency and a struggle for survival. We are told by the Prime Minister that we must face a reduction of the living standards of the Canadian people. I just want to bring to the attention of the house how certain corporations face this situation at this time. I want to quote, from a few reports and from a few newspaper items that I think are quite reliable, the opinion of certain companies regarding the prospects for the reduction of profits in the year ahead. As long as the present state of international tension continues to exist, the demand for farm implements will, in all probability, be strongly sustained.

Rouyn looks for record year in 1951-growing production levels, higher prices, outlook bright.

Defence Production Act that had to do with armed services preparedness. This is what is stated in the article: The recently adopted order limiting the use of nickel for civilian purposes is official acknowledgment of the growing scarcity of this vital metal. Why is there such a scarcity?

In the light of the allegations made in the complaint . . . the consent decree did almost nothing to affect the basic monopoly Inco enjoys over the sale of nickel and nickel products in the United States.

Apparently because the company is Canadian the United States department of justice felt compelled to accept a settlement on terms giving far less relief than requested.
The Johnson committee declared that Inco is so typically an unregulated monopoly that it could serve well as a case study. I continue with the quotation:
The company gives no indication that it intends to change its position. Its past behaviour, as the Johnson Senate committee points out, is typical of unregulated monopoly. This article deals at great length with this situation. I want to mention here that while the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) says we face a struggle for survival, we face a great national emergency, this great monopoly, according to a committee of the United States senate, refuses to expand production to meet the emergency.
Further the article states a recommendation was made by that committee that the matter be taken up with the Canadian government to see if it could do anything to get the International Nickel Company to expand production. United States government and what action has been taken to get the International Nickel to co-operate with our defence production effort.	.
We cannot defend freedom, Mr. Speaker, and continue to chant the litanies of the countinghouse, or approach the struggle for survival in the spirit of the money changers. While these companies from their balance sheets and from the statements of their officers and as a result of an investigation by one senate committee in the United States with respect to International Nickel indicate that they expect higher profits, while living standards fall, the Canadian people are told by the Prime Minister that they must accept a lower standard of living. In my opinion the Canadian people will accept the sacrifice that is necessary to defend freedom provided that sacrifice is on the basis of equality. That has been the attitude of this group throughout the years. Its attitude has been that in any national emergency the national effort in all its phases should be on the basis of equality of sacrifice. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would urge upon this government a political understanding and approach that will reflect the public understanding of the principles of democracy, and their opposition to any association with war criminals and people of that ilk.
I further suggest with respect to the economic aspects of this program that the government still do something to equalize the burden of the defence effort program by the reinstatement of price controls and subsidies that the Canadian people have been urging by rationing of goods in short supply when that is necessary; by a policy that will provide houses for thousands of Canadians in the lower income groups who need them badly now; and by establishing a rate of taxation when the budget is brought down that will prevent all profiteering and make our defence effort a real co-operative effort; also by the decentralization of industry and by the use of production potential of the smaller industrialists in this country.
In my plea for equal treatment of the Canadian people, and the placing of the burden with some degree of equality, I am reminded of a quotation from Burke. It is strange that I have to return to a former Conservative to finish my argument. The quotation is as follows:
Justice is itself the standing policy of civil society, and any departure from it under any circumstances lies under the suspicion of being no policy at all.
If our defence production program is not based on the principle of equality of sacrifice it will be no policy at all so far as effects are concerned. Throughout the years this group has defended the principle of equality

of sacrifice in every field in a national emergency, and will continue to do so. To demonstrate its faith in democracy and the principles of justice this government's program must at least demand equality of sacrifice.

I wish to take only two or three minutes at this time, in the hope that the minister will clear up one matter which is disturbing me.
In principle the bill before us asks for very wide and comprehensive powers to set up a Department of Defence Production. I am inclined to think such a department is needed, and I shall vote for it. I think it is apparent that such a department is needed when we look at some of the defence production figures which have been given to us in recent weeks.
The Korean war has been going on for about nine months. Thus far, apparently, Canadian rearming is progressing at a very slow rate. In the house on February 5, the Minister of National Defence put on Hansard figures that I cannot reconcile. He said this:
In the first nine months of the present fiscal year, which ended on December 31, 1950, 80,000 orders were actually placed with industry.
I suppose those orders were placed by the Department of Trade and Commerce. The minister then continued:
During this period orders have been placed with trade and commerce for the sum of $701 million.
The main items are:
Aircraft, $331 million; ships, $96 million: radar and wireless, $50 million; clothing and textiles, $35 million; motor vehicles, $50 million.
On February 26, about three weeks later, a reply was tabled to a question I had asked about motor production. My question was:
1.	Since June, 1950, have any defence contracts been placed with (a) Ford Motor Company; (b) General Motors; (c) Chrysler Motor Corporation; (d) Studebaker of Canada?
2.	If so, what was the dollar value of contracts placed with each company?
The answer I received stated that defence orders of less than $2,500,000 had been placed with the motor industry-in other words less than five per cent of the figure the minister had given two weeks earlier. Are we to assume from these figures that our defence program so far is still a program on paper only? Many Canadians fear that such is the
Defence Production Act case. If only five per cent of motor contracts reported have been actually placed, is the same true of ships, is the same true of radar, is the same true of aircraft?
I suppose that the department to be set up by this measure will ensure that defence contracts are placed more rapidly. However, before we go further, I believe the minister should tell us the present position of our defence production-the proportion which is on paper only, and the proportion which has actually been given out to industry. The figures to which I have referred are startling, and I cannot reconcile them.

Mr. Speaker, already the point of view of our party has been stated by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I should like to go over some of the ground he has covered, most certainly not for the purpose of in any way seeking to explain his extremely clear and excellent analysis of the bill, but rather so that I may keep the remarks I wish to make in consecutive order in relation to the bill itself.
As the hon. member told the house, a distinction must be drawn between the principle of any bill and the details of that bill which can be discussed in committee, and at which time amendments can be proposed. The principle of the bill was set forth in the statement made earlier this afternoon by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). He said correctly that the effect of the bill, if it became law, would be to produce three important results. One would be that it would establish the Department of Defence Production, another that it would confer powers on the minister to carry out the duties of that department, and the third that it would confer on the minister and the government authority to control and direct supplies as well as to take the appropriate steps to assure the production of defence requirements.
It seems to me the principle we have under consideration in the debate on second reading is whether or not in the opinion of the house there should be a department of defence production, and whether that department should have the appropriate powers to carry out its duties. Naturally the existence of any department calls for the appointment of a minister and for the setting up of the necessary staff to operate the department, which is in fact covered by the bill.
In so far as the bill sets up a department of defence production and gives proper authority to carry out the appropriate duties of that department, I feel sure there is approval throughout the whole of the house.

Defence Production Act I would say that there is more than approval, that there is a feeling of great urgency, and that as has already been pointed out by one hon. member the time is long overdue for the production of certain defence requirements which the country was promised long ago.
Let me give one example of the reason for concern that should be in the minds of all hon. members. This subject has been referred to before, but I believe there should be reference to it again in relation to the purpose of the bill, because it is so closely associated with the reasons why steps should be taken to set up a department of this kind. It was two years ago this Easter that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) made the important announcement that the Canadian government had decided to adopt the .300 calibre weapons of the United States, and to produce machine guns and rifles of the .300 calibre, which is the standard of the United States army, as well as to adopt as our standard certain equipment used by the forces of that country, so that there could be a closer integration of our activities.
It was certainly a cause for very real concern by every Canadian who had been reassured by that statement that something was going to be done-whether they agreed with the decision to adopt the American calibre or not-when we learned that publicly-owned arsenals in this country capable of producing very large quantities of machine guns and rifles had been making sporting weapons, while we had been selling our .303 calibre weapons to countries in different parts of the world, including the agents of communist China.
I do not see how it is possible to have any feeling but the feeling that there is something approaching criminal neglect when we see that, in the face of these emergencies which are so constantly impressed upon us by the government, it fails to use the productive capacity already owned by the state to produce the weapons we need so badly, and which are needed not only by the active force but also by the reserve force, about which during the present session there has already been discussion in the house.

I know that it has been under consideration for some time and that a decision may not be easy to make, but certainly it is a decision that is very urgently required. Because we believe that there should be a Department of Defence Production with the appropriate agencies to carry it into effect we will support the principle of the bill on second reading. For reasons which have already been very carefully put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), that does not imply acceptance of the details of the bill or of many of the provisions which we regard as entirely out of keeping at this time with the arguments put forward by the government with respect to other measures under consideration, and entirely out of keeping with the attempt that is being made to create the impression in the house that we should not act as though we were yet fully engaged in something of the nature of a general war.
We have indicated our own belief that emphasis should be placed on the fact that the preparations taking place are preparations which we hope will result in peace. We believe, however, that everything should proceed as rapidly as possible but under proper supervision of parliament. In presenting the criticisms which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra directed to certain sections of the bill, he made it clear he was hoping that by bringing these criticisms forward in detail at this time the government might consider the advisability of amending many of these sections before we are called upon to deal with the bill in committee, and that the government would voluntarily come before the house and present a bill which in fact retains the responsibility of parliament over the things that are to be done by this defence production board.
Every effort has been made by the government to create the impression that we must not proceed as though we were in a state of war, and with that I agree. The achievement of peace should be the goal towards which anything that we do is directed, but this act is drafted as though we were already in a more terrible war than that in which we became involved in September, 1939. In some respects this act confers more arbitrary
Defence Production Act powers than did the legislation which this government saw fit to introduce during the most terrible war that has been known in all the history of the world. I think it is essential that, in considering the extent to which the bill now goes and why we urge in all earnestness that the government redraft the bill with recognition that we should continue the authority of parliament during a period of an emergency which may extend for long years, we should recognize the arguments that have been put before the people of Canada outside the house by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and his associates. For that reason I should like to quote the exact words of the Prime Minister from a speech outside the house, it is true, but here in the city of Ottawa the day before yesterday. I shall quote from the exact text of his speech. At one point he said:
Nothing is easier than to assume that because there is some resemblance between the circumstances of today and the circumstances of eleven or twelve years ago the same course of action is called for.
We must not forget that we are not trying to win the second world war today. Today we are trying to prevent a third world war. That too is going to require a tremendous effort. But it is going to be different in many ways from what we were doing ten or eleven years ago. Some of the things we did then do have to be done again. But other things called for to win a shooting war are completely unsuited to the task of preventing a shooting war.
There the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was seeking to emphasize the fact that we should not now be called upon in parliament to confer upon the government emergency measures with as wide authority as some of those that were regarded as necessary in that war which began more than ten years ago. Then at a later point in the same speech he had something else to say which I think is worth reading into the record at this point because this speech obviously was intended as a statement to the people of Canada in relation to a subject under consideration in this house. Later on the Prime Minister said:
The most serious domestic problem we face is inflation. That was a serious problem ten years ago and it is a serious problem today. I suppose the consequence of inflation which creates the greatest anxiety for most men and women- especially with families-is the rising cost of living. And the increase in the cost of living is a very real anxiety to the government, too.
Almost ten years ago, the government of the day undertook to keep down the cost of living while the war was on by establishing price ceilings. Our wartime price control policy was an outstanding success. For that very reason it is hard for many people to understand why we are not able to do in 1951 what worked so well after 1941. And you may be sure we would adopt the same policy now if we believed it would really work. But would it? It is true prices were rising in 1941

and they are rising in 1951; but many other conditions in 1951 are very different from those we faced in 1941.
In 1941 the war was on. Our aim was to devote the maximum effort of our people to winning it as quickly as possible. To do that we were cutting out all non-essential activities and distributing the essentials as evenly as possible.

May I emphasize those last words. I have read this extended quotation into the record because it indicates the attitude of the government, and we regard that attitude as not facing the full realities in many respects. The government refuse to do some of these other things because they say we should not go so far today; yet when the bill is brought down dealing with the whole economy of Canada, no matter what the purpose may be we find that it actually goes further than did the legislation introduced by this' same government during the course of that most terrible war which ended in 1945.
In the consideration of the emergency powers legislation the Prime Minister sought over and over again to impress upon the house that he would not wish to ask for powers of the type required in actual war. Why, then, does this bill ask for greater powers than were asked by this government in an actual all-out war such a short time ago? I think perhaps the answer to that is to be found in the words of the minister this afternoon, and I quote his exact words: "I have supervised the drafting of this bill." In describing the bill, the minister frankly stated that it contained powers of an extraordinary nature; but, as has been pointed out, there was no explanation as to why those extraordinary powers are required at this time to do the things we all agree should be done, and very quickly. The obvious fact is that the minister sees no reason to explain. The government has a huge majority. The minister decides that this should be done; he obtains the consent of the government, and he knows that the vote will support what is before this house. Consequently the rest of us, and I suppose the members of his party as well, have no need to be told why action of this kind should be taken at this time. Surely in the light of what is before us there can be no other explanation of the fact that powers so wide as these should be required.
It seems to me that for this reason every member of this house should seek to understand what actually is the full effect of this legislation. This bill certainly confers powers which go further than powers parliament should confer upon any government or any 

minister without a great deal more explanation than we have had so far. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has referred to one extraordinary section relating to these extraordinary powers. That is section 5, which reads:
The minister may authorize any person, on his behalf and under his control and direction, to do any act or thing or to exercise any power that the minister may do or exercise under this act.
It is in relation to this section that we should read1 the powers the minister really has. As he indicated, the minister has power to create crown corporations for the purpose of carrying out the objects of this legislation. That is covered- by section 7, and in subsection 3 of that section we find this-:
The minister may remove any members, directors, or officers- of a corporation incorporated under this section at any time and may appoint others in their stead or may appoint additional persons as members.
Referring back to section 5, therefore, we find that this is not something to be done by order in council, but that corporations with immense capital, and of great importance to all Canada, may have their officers removed and other officers appointed, not by the minister, although he is named, but by any Tom, Dick or Harry authorized by the minister, utterly unknown to this house. So we are conferring upon the minister not only the power to do these extraordinary things, in many cases without the approval of the government itself; we are still further asked to let him name anyone and give him authority to exercise these tremendous powers which may so greatly affect the future of Canada. Then again we find in section 11 that it is not the government by order in council but the minister who-
-shall examine Into, organize, mobilize, and conserve the resources of Canada contributory to, and the sources of supply of, defence supplies and the agencies and facilities available for the supply of the same. . .
Then it goes on to explain that this power shall extend to construction projects and the exploration of all the possibilities in that field. There again, it is not the government upon whom we are conferring a power, nor the minister alone, but someone unknown to the government, unknown to parliament, who may be appointed by the minister at any time to undertake this task. This same extension of power goes right on through the act.
Section 23, which is a section of immense power, provides the following, and I think in the text of what I am saying I shall read this section. It reads:
(1) Where a person who has been requested to enter into a defence contract on terms and conditions that the minister considers to be fair and reasonable has refused or failed to enter into the

contract, if the minister is satisfied that such person owns or controls facilities that are suitable for or can be adapted to the work required to carry out such contract and that his refusal or failure was without reasonable excuse, the minister may direct that person to produce, deliver or store, or to construct, as the case may be, on such terms and conditions and within such period as the minister considers to be fair and reasonable in the circumstances, the defence supplies or the defence project or projects that would have been the subject matter of the contract if it had been entered into.
(2) A person who stores defence supplies pursuant to a direction under this section is liable for the loss thereof or for damage thereto as if he had agreed to store them for reward.
Think of the powers conferred under that section, and then recognize that under section 5 we are asked to authorize the minister to place powers of that kind under no restraint of government, let alone parliament, in the hands of anyone who may be appointed by the minister at any time on his own discretion.
Then, section 28 is another section of great importance. Again, so that my remarks carry through the effect of this bill in sequence so far as the powers of the minister being delegated are concerned, I shall read section 28. It reads:
(1)	The minister may, by order, direct that a person shall not be bound-
I should like those members who are still interested in the responsibility of parliament, and in the authority of provincial legislatures as well as municipal councils, to listen to the effect of these words:

by any obligation, restriction or limitation imposed on that person by or under any statute, order, rule, regulation, by-law, or contract with respect to such matters as may be specified in the order affecting the entry into or performance of a defence contract by that person or the carrying out of an order made by the minister under this act.
(2)	Where the failure to fulfil any contract, whether entered into before or after the commencement of this act, is due to the compliance on the part of any person with any provision of this act or any order or regulation, proof of that fact shall be a good defence to any action or proceeding in respect of the failure.
There is no necessity, Mr. Speaker, to try to extend the interpretation of this to any particular limit. It is only necessary to see what this actually means. This is not power by order in council, dangerous though that may be, but this means that under section 5 any person without legal training, without business training, without knowledge of the subject matter at all, if he happened to be appointed by the minister would have a power which would be greater than that of the legislatures of this country during the life of this act. This power conferred by section 28 would give that power to any individual, without the cabinet even knowing it, to override any dominion statute, provincial statute, any municipal bylaw or regulation or order made under them which affected any
Defence Production Act contract, or the subject matter relating to one of these defence contracts. It is not possible to conceive of a greater defiance of the responsibility of parliament than section 28.
Then, let us go to the next section, section 29.

Whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce drafted the bill or not, the Minister of Justice is the minister responsible for legislation introduced by the government; and even at the dreadful risk of being once again in disagreement with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I do urge him to accept his responsibility as Minister of Justice of a democratic parliament, and to redraft this bill before we go into committee so that we shall still have responsible government in Canada and so that hon. members of this house and of the parliament of Canada shall retain some control over the destiny of our country.

In war I submit that we give extraordinary powers for two reasons, first of all, because it is war and we are in danger. We are ready to do almost anything for security. But there is another and very important reason, namely, because there is a natural time for the powers to end. We give the powers with the feeling that they are temporary, and that the time will come when everyone will agree that they should end. I submit that today the situation is radically different from that. We have been told again and again by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton)-well, by almost everyone who has spoken about it-that we must face this situation as a situation that may go on for a very long time. And yet-and I submit this with the hope that members on the government side of the house will consider it carefully-what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) says is true, that we are asked here to give these extraordinary powers. The minister himself said earlier this afternoon that they are extraordinary powers. Therefore I think it is the duty of every one of us, having had that mentioned, to ask whether all these extraordinary powers are necessary.

The leader of the opposition has referred particularly to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). I wish to point out that in this chamber last night the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Justice seemed to me to set a very fine example in trying to meet a situation so that the judgment of the house would be carried. They did not just say, "We have drafted this bill, and we will not change a word of it". There was what I think the whole country would approve, a- real measure of trying to find a solution which if possible would be satisfactory to all.
Now, it is not a figure of speech-and I hope that even the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will not push it aside, as he so often has pushed aside what I have said before, as theory-it is not a figure of speech to say that if this goes on long enough and that if these powers, these extraordinary and amazing powers-and I confess I had not realized the full extent of them, and did not realize the extent to which provincial and municipal jurisdiction has been swept aside, or potentially so, until I listened to my leader-I think it is not any exaggeration to say that if these amazing powers go on for five, ten, fifteen or twenty years, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) says, we will have a generation of businessmen who do not know what freedom is. This is a rather unusual case, and I think the attention of the house and the country should be drawn to it. As the hon. member has just said, it is not to our credit that we rush through divorce bills in this way. In other words, we allow parliament to become a place for cleaning the linen of domestic tribulation from one of the provinces. I sat here last session, I believe it was, and saw a bill go through along with a number of others without any questions being asked. To my personal knowledge, in granting the divorce in that case we made ourselves parties to inflicting great suffering upon an innocent child, a crippled boy who was wearing iron supports on his legs, a little lad of five or six years of age. In addition there was a very innocent little girl.
Their mother abandoned them. Their father was a Royal Canadian Air Force officer, and we were in the unhappy position of passing

that measure without any comment at all or any query. The mother went away with another man and left the children to become objects of pity. If there is no sanctity to marriage we might as well close up parliament because parliament is based upon the proposition that we have established homes in the country. You cannot have a parliament when people are nomads travelling about on horses gathering up women in one town and carrying them on to the next. Parliament is based on the idea of the sanctity of the home and upon the fact of course that Canada is a Christian country. Marriage vows must be taken seriously if marriages are to endure. Of course Hollywood and other places have a very low standard in that respect.
In the case before us are we prepared to pass over this matter lightly, without asking anything about the parties? Hidden in this case is a drama equal to anything in the literature of Greece or Rome. If we lightly pass over these things we destroy the foundations not only of our church and our families, but of parliament. This woman has gone away with a certain American who is known to be a leader among the communists of the United States, who is known to have given money for the carrying on of subversive communistic activities in the United States. He is the son of a very wealthy Chicago family, a man who has had the benefit of everything possible in the way of luxury, education and culture that either the United States or the Canadian system could give. He took this woman away with him to the United States. Whether or not they are living in bigamy is not of any interest to me but I say to this committee that it should pause and closely analyse this bill before making the parliament of Canada a party to the project which is being proposed.

The hon. member for Cariboo has levelled a pretty damning indictment against the woman in this case, Mrs. Boyer. If she is the guilty party and Mr. Boyer has been wronged in the way the hon. member for Cariboo says he has, I ask why Mr. Boyer should be made to suffer. This parliament is not being asked to do anything at the request of Mrs. Boyer. We are being asked to grant relief to Mr. Boyer. It seems to me the other circumstances relating to Mr. Boyer do not come into the picture at all.
The fact of the matter is that though members may disagree with divorce, though I may not like it-and I hope none of us likes it-nevertheless it is within the power of this parliament to pass acts of this kind, and these people have the right under the British North America Act to come to parliament and ask for these acts. So long as that right is there, so long as these people have no other recourse, I do not see how parliament can refuse to grant the relief these people seek, so long as they can prove their right in each individual case. Nor do I see that it is any solution to the problem just to get up and walk out of the committee or, as I hear the hon. member for Lethbridge saying, just to talk about it. I am one member of the house, at any rate, who can say something about this matter, because I have proposed a concrete 
method whereby divorces from the provinces where the majority of the people do not want divorce courts could be dealt with in some other way than by parliament. It is very heroic for hon. members to get up and make these pious speeches about how sick and tired they are of this practice, but that reminds me of the old story about the weather. Let us not just talk about it; let us do something about it.
I have made my suggestion; indeed I put it before the house on two occasions in the form of a bill. Apparently it was not acceptable to the Prime Minister and others in this house, though I felt that perhaps it was misunderstood. My proposal was that in the case of persons residing in provinces where there are no divorce courts, divorce actions should be tried by the Exchequer Court of Canada. My thought in that connection was that this was a court that could stay here in Ottawa to hear these cases, and thereby would not be sitting within the provinces where the majority of the people do not want divorce courts; yet it would make available to the people in those provinces who required that relief the opportunity to obtain more properly the right which at present can be granted only by parliament.
If my proposal is not acceptable I suggest to the hon. member for Battle River, the hon. member for Medicine Hat, the hon. member for Ottawa East who just walked out, and any others who do not like it, that they come forward with a better proposal. I am glad to learn that some of the hon. members I have mentioned supported my proposal last year, but I think responsibility does rest upon individual members and upon the government to face up to this issue and find some other way. Let us not try to escape from the whole problem by thinking that if parliament is not prepared to find some other way we are going to deny these people who need this relief a right which is in the British North America Act. Section 91 provides that this parliament has the right to make laws with respect to marriage and divorce.
Frankly I do not see why this fuss should be raised with respect to this one case, particularly when that fuss was based upon the fact that the guilty party-and the hon. member for Cariboo says "very guilty"-is not the one we are asked to accommodate. This bill provides relief for the innocent party, in the manner in which he is by law entitled to it.

I am not making any charges. I am saying that this is a very important, outstanding and very dramatic case. This is a modern interpretation of Samson and Delilah. I do not think that the
