In the last eighty years legislation to create divorce courts in the different provinces has been brought before the house. The province of Alberta has such courts, and so has the province of Ontario. Today there are only two provinces in which the citizens have to apply to the dominion parliament to get relief. These divorce bills are brought before a Senate committee which listens to the evidence. This committee grants or rejects the request. The evidence is taken in shorthand and published. Copies of that evidence are sent to the members of parliament, who may or may not study each case. The bill then goes to the House of Commons, receives first and second reading and is referred to the committee on private bills. This committee goes over the evidence, calls witnesses and listens to both parties. Then it renders a decision. The bill is then referred back to the house, to the committee of the whole. Members may speak or put questions to the sponsors of those bills, and elicit all the information they wish. When a vote is called, if members do not like them why do they not vote against them?
In the twenty-one years in which I have been sitting in the house, I think there have been only two or three instances in which divorce bills have been thrown out. If this bill were voted upon, I would vote against it, both on principle and on the evidence. It all comes back to the fact that members who are not living in the province of Quebec want to tell us the way in which we should proceed with divorces. We are not yet ready to admit what they say about divorce courts. Even if we did try to establish divorce courts in the province of Quebec, the local government would not set up the court. In such an event the minority in the province would have no way of getting relief. The majority may be Catholic, but there is a minority. I do not know how this minority in the province of Quebec who believe in divorce could be dealt with. We would have to let them have some way of obtaining relief.
At every session this question seems to be brought forward. On the suggestion of the member for Winnipeg North Centre a committee was set up to consider it. The question seems to be difficult, because the committee did not arrive at any conclusion. In almost every session we spend three, four, or five hours trying to pass divorce bills to

I know that is not the opinion of the majority in this house, but it is my opinion. Most members believe that if someone is wronged he should have a right of redress. Now, you may speak in any terms, but before you can change the jurisdiction this parliament has over divorce you have to do a lot of work amongst the Catholics, and amongst the people of the province of Quebec.

speechtext:
As he is not
here I should like to blame the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). Anything I say that is bad I hope will be attributed to him, and if I say anything that is good I shall be very glad to take the credit myself.
The first thing that I wish to say is that I think we, through nobody's fault and nobody's intention, were hustled into this bill; or, at any rate, we blundered into it without giving it the consideration which I think it deserves. I confess myself to being out for a few minutes when the bill was brought down, and it was nearly all over when I got in. If it had not been for the hon. member for Cape Breton South, and one or two others, the bill would be law now.
The first thing that strikes me is that I have not been able to make out that there is any argument for it, except what I call the week-end argument; that is to say, that it would be more convenient to have the holiday come on a Monday, because it is more convenient to have holidays on Monday, and have the day thrown in with Saturday and Sunday.
Well, I admit that that is an argument, and I think if you put that argument suddenly, and without any previous consideration, to a
Statutory Holidays
vast number of voters they would be inclined to say, yes, that is a good idea. But I equally believe that if you took the time to discuss it with a thoughtful citizen he would begin to doubt whether it is such a good idea after all. Perhaps I feel that because it expresses my own mental history in this matter. The question is therefore to ask ourselves:	Is it
just another week end, or is there something of value in it?
I recall again the point which the hon. member for Cape Breton South made which I thought was very sound. He said:	"What
do you think would happen if you asked the ordinary American, or even the extraordinary American, what he would think of casually changing the celebration of the fourth of July to some other day?" He answered the question, as I think we would probably all answer it: We think the ordinary American would toss the idea out of the window pretty quickly.
Perhaps we may sometimes feel that Americans are a little-what shall I say-excitable, a little too dramatic about these matters; but on the whole I feel that the Americans have done a very good job of taking immigrants of the widest possible variety and turning them into pretty good American citizens.
It may be objected, and I think properly so, that in England there is nothing that just corresponds to this; at least I never could discover that there was. But I think there is a reason for that. They have many centuries of history behind them. They have a great homogeneity. They have all their own local customs that go back for hundreds of years, and yet they are integrated in the large sense, too. I think that is the reason that they have not felt it necessary. But I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in, this country of ours we are as different as can be from them.
I doubt whether there is any country that has more need of celebrating and remembering and trying to cherish and to magnify whatever things of any nature we have that draw us together. I should like to read a brief extract from the book that I hold in my hand, written by a man whose name has been mentioned in this house recently, namely, the Right Hon. Vincent Massey, the chairman of the so-called Massey commission. He wrote a book which is entitled "On being Canadian", and he has a paragraph in that book I should like to read from, and which I think is interesting. He says:
If "the man from Mars" (whose detached views are always so useful) could see us, what would he think of our future as a community? He would see fewer than thirteen millions of people widely scattered over half a continent, more than three-quarters of them living in a ribbon of settlements, broken here and there by wilderness, within two hundred miles of the border between ourselves

Statutory Holidays
and a country nearly twelve times our size with all the physical attraction and the powerful influences which a large body exerts on a small one. He would note that here and there our best roads lead to the south. He would observe that our two leading cities are more than 300 miles apart;
And then skipping some, I read again:
There are forty-two Canadian periodicals carrying advertisements in foreign languages of which thirteen are represented. The Bible is distributed in Canada in over fifty languages. Such is the variety of our racial composition.
And then he says:
With all the difficulties that confront us, would our Martian have some doubts about our future as a nation? Our own confidence should be powerfully reinforced by our success up to the present.
And then he says:
And we have a meaning, however often we may forget it.
I would like to pick up that phrase, "We have a meaning", and to ask, if that is so, whether it does not suggest to us that perhaps we should develop that meaning, and whether this Dominion day is not part of the pattern-and I do not want to press it- but perhaps it is a small part of the pattern, one of the vehicles evolved to help us. I raise that question.
I should like to say, and I think it is true, that Dominion day, confederation, was the greatest achievement of the two original races in Canada, and I am glad to find, having asked French-Canadian members in the house, that le jour de la confederation is respected and celebrated in the province of Quebec. I hope very much that people who can speak on the subject with more authority than I can will be able to say, if it is true-and I believe it is-that it is acquiring significance among our newer citizens. And if that is so, as I think it is, then it seems to me that we should not lightly pass it aside and regard it as just another week end.
I was impressed when the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) told us the other night what had been done by the late Mr. McGeer, who was a member of the other place, and whom we all remember as a man of great vigour and' patriotism. He thought it was worth while, apparently despite a good deal of scepticism, to organize in Vancouver a celebration of Dominion day on a scale that had not been done before; and apparently it was a great success.
My feeling is that that is an example we might well follow, that we should cherish and magnify it, and not throw it away. I repeat what I said a moment ago, that I doubt if there is any country which should stress more the common ties that it has than should our country. I cannot help hoping that the House of Commons will take this matter more

seriously than it seemed* likely to do when the subject was first presented. I feel we ought to be able to give a bit of a lead here.
I said a few moments ago, and I believe it, that if you accosted the ordinary voter who had not given the matter any thought, and suggested to him that the day be changed to Monday, I think he would be inclined to say, "Yes; a good idea". But I do feel, as I said before, that if he were asked to think it over for a few moments he would not be nearly so sure; and I think further that if one undertook to make a bit of an argument with him, even as modest as the one I make now, at the end of five or ten minutes he would say, "It is not a good idea at all".
I would remind hon. members that we have a great advantage in the House of Commons. We come down here and1 take part in ceremonies which, I think, impress us very much, ceremonies embedded deep not only in our past but in a past which goes beyond ours. I do not find that people take those things lightly. I believe that, whatever may be the feelings of members when they arrive here, whether they think of them as a lot of fuss and feathers, they become converted, and rather quickly. I have heard no one who has treated them lightly, and I think they come to feel that, behind the dignity of those ceremonies, there is something that goes deeper.
If I am right in that, then I think those of us who have that advantage, one which is not shared by so many of the citizens of Canada, should consider carefully before we do anything which in my opinion would destroy, or at least go far to destroy an institution of great value.
After all, our whole civilization depends upon the belief, the faith and the mental attitude of a great body of citizens. As I said a moment ago, I believe that this celebration, inadequate as it is, should be kept; that it is part of the pattern-a small part, if you like-but certainly a part of the pattern of our life. As I have said, it represents, I believe, the greatest achievement of the two races. That, in itself, is a very great thing.
Lastly I should like to say this. If this is true in ordinary times, then how much truer is it today. Surely we must recognize, as we never did before, that our whole system, our whole civilization, is facing a task. It is facing an organization-and we may use any unpleasant adjective that we wish-but it is an organization which, nevertheless, has a certain toughness, a certain queer, perverted and inverted faith which we have to match with other beliefs and other moral strengths which, in the main, we have to get out of our background and out of our history.

I suggest that this day, which we have come to regard as part of our history-and I am speaking of Dominion day-is a serious part of our lives. I hope very much that there will be others who will join me in speaking in the debate. I shall not abandon hope that members in the house from all parties may, before it is too late, come to the conclusion which I have come to, rather late, I confess, that there is something here -which is worthy of being preserved, and which is more than just another week end.

Mr. Speaker, seeing that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) is in a flexible frame of mind, and that he has appealed to members to express their opinions, may I say that I am not a convert. I would suggest to him that the great church festival we are now approaching, the festival of Easter, loses nothing in its solemnity because it changes from one month to another.
I am not impressed a bit by the argument that, because Dominion day was held on some day other than the first day of July, it would lose any of its national importance. Easter day is Easter day, no matter whether it falls in March or in April. Dominion day will always be Dominion day whether we celebrate it on the first, second, third or fourth day of the month. I discard the emphasis placed upon the holding of every festival on some particular day of the month. I have to be realistic, and I ask myself what do the people of my constituency wish. I am quite certain that the tourist camps on Vancouver island hope that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and his friends from Vancouver will come and spend a long week end on the island, but what is far more important is that the men working in logging camps high up on the mountain sides want the long week ends so that they *can go back to their families either on the seaboard or on the mainland of British Columbia. They would much rather do that over a long week end than pay for extra meals while lying around logging camps on a Wednesday or Thursday.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was drawing its attention to some of the defects, as I thought, in the bill now before us. I had suggested that the powers given in the bill were virtually going to turn the business of the country into an economy living by the grace of one man, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I was wrong in one particular. I should not have said one man. I should have said one man and a host of delegates of that one man, which on the whole makes the thing much worse because can we believe that we are going to have a large number of men who have the qualities of experience, knowledge, wisdom, moderation and single-mindedness that are going to be necessary to exercise these far-reaching and virtually unlimited powers described to us this afternoon by my leader?
Is that not expecting too much, Mr. Speaker? Are we not merely going to fool ourselves if we do 'that? That is the reason why I said this afternoon I was not going to abandon hope that in the case of this measure the minister might be prepared to do something like what was done last evening by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in making alterations in the emergency powers bill. I hope the same thing may be done with this measure.
I also spoke of freedom, and I should like to make this further comment that if by our own act we destroy our freedom it is a kind of suicide which would be much worse than physical suicide because I think we can say that people of our country do value freedom more than anything in the world. I know it is awfully hard to make people, who have never known a country where, except in an emergency, there was any restriction on freedom, believe that it could ever be serious. Of course we know that our enemies believe -and I think genuinely-that the stresses we are going to be put under in this cold war or semi-twilight war, or whatever you wish to call it, are going to be so severe that they indulge in the hope that it may break down the things that we really care about. I have no doubt as Russian agents follow our debates, as they are no doubt doing, that they must be very pleased indeed to feel that we find it necessary, if we are going to find it necessary, to resort to powers almost incredible in peacetime.
If I remember rightly the minister himself referred to them this afternoon as extraordinary, and if he regards them as extraordinary we can be sure they are because

Defence Production Act he is quite an expert in powers himself, and I would accept his view on that subject.
With this background I should like to look at some of the practical workings of the bill. I said this afternoon that I thought the situation has a good deal of similarity superficially with the situation which existed during wartime, and also a good deal of dissimilarity. I hope to be able to show that the dissimilarity is much greater than the similarity. Of course the similarity is1 obvious enough. The minister is going to be asked to supply ships, planes, tanks and guns, all the same kind of things that he supplied: during the last war. I realize that, and I think that similarity has naturally impressed the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I do not think it was very hard for him to be impressed, and I think he has not felt it necessary to ask himself any very searching questions as to the dissimilarity.
I should like to say that I think the situation today is just as dissimilar as it can be. In the first place we are not at war. I take it-and I am sure the minister will agree with this part of my speech-that in wartime you have all kinds of unexpected situations to deal with. Ships are being torpedoed. Battles are being won and lost. Equipment in huge amounts is disappearing in unexpected ways, either by torpedoing or by loss in battle. New situations are arising. Perhaps new allies are coming in or some allies are being knocked out. I take it that every conceivable kind of situation has to be faced. One might say that the keynote is uncertainty, and I can imagine that with all the uncertainty of those days there may have been reasons for special powers which I suggest very earnestly do not exist today.
In wartime the minister had powers, and I particularly want to refer to the powers proposed under section 16 of the bill, the financial section. First I want to go back and make clear why I think the situation today is so dissimilar. I tried to indicate that in wartime uncertainty was the keynote, that the minister never knew very far ahead just what his task was, and that all kinds of unexpected things could arise for which it was fair and right that he should have unexpected powers. What is the situation now? The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) came into the house some three weeks ago and outlined to us in considerable detail the program of defence production over the next three years. He went into' very great detail. We were told about planes, guns, ships and so on. After setting out his requirements in considerable detail the

Minister of National Defence said, as recorded at page 95 of Hansard:
This1 report indicates something of the size of the equipment program now under way and gaining momentum from day to day.
Then he added:
To meet these requirements a new department of the government, the Department of Defence Production, is being proposed.
What I wish to stress is that there is all the difference in the world between the task the minister had roughly ten years ago and the task he has now. The task then, as I said, was full of uncertainties, full of unexpected situations. I have no doubt that if the minister cared to do so he could give us many illustrations of how his problems changed from month to month and indeed quite often from day to day. Here none of these elements are present, as far as I can see. True, no one can foresee the future. Within a month, if certain unhoped-for things should arise, the situation might be different, but I think we are entitled to take the situation as it is today; and the situation as it is today is that for the next three years-and incidentally I hope this legislation will not cover any period longer than that-the minister is asked to make preparations, to get the materials and let the contracts to take care of a defence program which he now knows and which, unless there are untoward international events, is not likely to be altered substantially. I suggest that is just as different from the task the minister had in wartime as chalk is from cheese, and that there is no basis in reason and common sense for the same powers to be asked now, in peacetime, to do a task which is known, which is definite and which, subject to the qualification I made, is not likely to change.
This house is the judge, and I can only hope that these grave questions will not be decided with a careless laugh and the slogan "Good old C. D.", which as far as I can make out is the basis on which a vote on this subject was given last year. In the proper circumstances I could say "Good old: C-. D." too, but I do noit think, as the old song says, it has anything to do with the case when we are dealing with serious matters. I would remind the minister and the house that after all, while he is free from many human weaknesses, he is not free from mortality, and we cannot guarantee that he will be permanently in this position even though the fortunes of his party should continue to prosper.
As I have said before, I hope parliament will not make this national emergency an occasion for setting up a private kingdom for

the minister. I want to remind hon. members of what was said earlier in the day, that the minister not only does not much like sharing his powers with parliament; he does not much like sharing his powers with members of his own party, and he has a great aversion to even sharing his powers with the cabinet. So we find that a very considerable number of those powers belong to the minister. I think I can understand why. I think the minister is the kind of man who has great power of decision, and he is not always wrong. I think he likes to make a decision without being held up by too much discussion, even in the cabinet. So when hon. members read this bill, as I hope they will, they will be perhaps a little astonished to find the number of powers held by the minister alone. Oh, there are some cases where the governor in council comes in, but I am inclined to think that most of the sections containing the most extravagant powers do not contain any dilution, and that the minister himself exercises those.
I should like to briefly illustrate what I mean when I say those powers are quite unnecessary, by referring to section 16, which is the monetary section and which sets up what is called a defence production revolving fund; I do not propose to quote the section. In brief, this fund in the first place gives the minister a little kitty of $100 million, which may be perfectly proper. Beyond that, however, it also gives him power to buy all kinds of materials related to defence; and as I said this afternoon, when you read the sections you find it very difficult to think of anything which is not covered in one way or another by defence. The minister has power to stockpile these things; he has power to act as agent for other governments, and he has power to make loans for various matters. Those are the outgoing amounts. Then there are various funds which come in. When he buys materials and sells them, of course that is money coming in. When he buys materials for a foreign government and the money comes back, that is a receipt; and there are other receipts which I need not go into. The point I want to make is that this fund, this kind of backlog of $100 million, through the various receipts and expenditures which would be permitted under the wide powers given the minister might very easily enable him over the course of a year to do hundreds of millions of dollars of business; and quite properly, too, provided there is a proper restriction on his power.
But I point out, Mr. Speaker, that as far as parliament is concerned we might as well be sitting in the moon, or in central Africa, for all we will ever know about it. No; I am
Defence Production Act wrong on one point. There is one qualification, one time the minister has to come back to parliament. That is when he sustains a loss. The section does say that when losses are sustained the minister really has to come back and tell us about them. That is very decent of him; I think we should be very grateful for that. When a loss is sustained, parliament does have to authorize it.
I want to stress that a bit, because as far as I understand, from such inquiries as I have been able to make, parliament will find out about all these interesting transactions when it sees the public accounts. Well, you know the child's old rhyme; this year, next year, some time, never. We get the public accounts, if I remember rightly, a good many months after the month of March in the year following the time these transactions take place. So in respect of transactions early in the year it would be nearly two years before we would get the information, though I suppose in some cases we might get the information in not much more than a year. That is why I say we might as well be sitting in the moon as far as any knowledge we may have of what is going on is concerned.
What is the need for that? In wartime, as I said earlier, we put up with a lot because we were frightened, and also because we felt that the emergency powers would come to a natural end when the war ended. But there is no natural end to this. If the world situation goes on as it well might, in this unsettled condition, this could mean five years or ten years, or as long as you want to imagine. I suggest that it does not seem very intelligent for people who spend a lot of time talking about freedom to give that power unless there is some strong reason for it. I would be quite open-minded, as evidently the members who-were in this house during the war were, in accepting the view in wartime that with the changes and vicissitudes which I tried to outline we should be very generous. We should be generous now, I think, but I do not. believe we should be downright silly and stupid, and just panic into giving power with out some reason as to why we should.
Let us look at the reason here. As I have tried to outline this to you, and I think it is fair, the minister starts off with $100 million, and with the various incomings and outgoings he will have he will be able, as I say, to have a kingdom of his own which we Will know nothing about because there is no provision for any reports as to the contracts which are to be made. Uniforms will be needed, let us say in the coming year of 1952. I understand, quite naturally, it will probably be almost routine that the department of defence production will lay in a lot of textile material to be used in the making of those uniforms. But for the life of me, I cannot understand why that cannot come in as an estimate of the department of defence production in the financial year 1951-52. I do not see why we need to have all this machinery, all these powers away off in a corner where nobody knows what is happening. I still hope the minister may take that view, or if he does not that parliament may take that view, and that members may ask why they cannot approve the figures in advance.
Now, let me put in one qualification. Even though the program is known, even though the minister can see three years ahead what his task is and what his requirements are going to be, there may be unexpected things which will come up. I believe there should be some leeway given, if necessary. Supposing that, contrary to my expectations, the minister should rise and say that was a reasonable suggestion by the member for Greenwood and that he would agree that he can put his requirements in estimates for the year 1951, but will need a certain amount of leeway for this and that. I believe that if the minister were as reasonable as I suggest he might possibly foe, I would be equally reasonable and suggest there should be some leeway. I say again that the more I study these wide powers and add them to the other sections which were particularly referred to this afternoon, the more it seems to me we are just taking a steam hammer to crack a nut.
The minister has these wide powers, and they are fine. It is rather dramatic to have wide powers; it is very convenient and very comfortable. I am sure the minister would be bored to death, having had the powers which he did have during the war, if he now had to go out and do a job which in some ways is similar without being clothed with


these almost godlike powers. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, taking this one section that I have mentioned as an illustration, I believe there is no earthly reason why these wide powers should be given. Even yet I hope the minister will to some extent agree. I have perhaps a tiny scintilla of hope that if the minister does not agree possibly his colleagues or some of his party members might still have some influence over him and prevent us from panicking into these powers. These powers are in contradiction of everything we say we believe in, and contrary to the oft-repeated principles of Liberalism which are being watered down so thin. They are contrary to what one wise man once called the immortal grounds of common sense.

In this respect, that I agree in principle with the setting up of this Department of Defence Production. I realize, as he does, that the minister in charge of the department must be given certain powers in order that teeth may be put into the legislation so as to enable him to produce the equipment so essential for our defence forces. Like him, I feel there should be no unnecessary powers, or powers which are not essential, given to the minister. That point has been dealt with, and I shall not refer to it again.
I am going to be perhaps presumptuous and offer a little advice to the minister, but in a very friendly way. I would draw to his attention the utmost importance of timing in this matter of defence production. I presume defence production will be linked closely with the three-year defence plan announced by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). Some of the equipment for those forces, in order that they may be made ready, is urgently needed and must be produced in the very shortest possible time. That applies particularly to those forces which are now, and which within the next few weeks will be, in Korea; and to those forces, including ground and air forces, which will be moving to Europe in the near future. It applies also to our airborne brigade which, here, may be required to meet a sudden emergency. It applies in so far as the reserve forces are concerned, particularly those of the army, because they must be given sufficient equipment to carry out their ordinary training.
In the past there has been some evidence of shortage of equipment. I am not going to elaborate upon it, but I feel that possibly the arrangements which had existed heretofore had not had sufficient teeth in them to enable the minister to procure, in the face of a booming civilian market, articles which are urgently needed. I hope that the rather leisurely methods which have been applied by the Canadian Commercial Corporation will be speeded up in certain respects so that manufacturers making equipment for the services will realize that it is a priority job, and that they must not let their service contracts take second place to more attractive civilian demands.
On the other hand, there is a great deal of equipment which is not so urgently needed and which can be produced after a lapse of time. There is always a danger that at the outbreak of a war your forces are so fully equipped that the equipment is obsolescent after a few months' time. Surely it is the history of all wars that the equipment with which you start a war is soon out of date. I fancy that I have noticed a trend in defence production which stresses the urgency of taking equipment off the production line no

Defence Production Act matter whether it is the very best or whether it is really urgently needed at the present time. "Let us equip our whole force" seems to have been almost the slogan of certain individuals. Therefore they have gone to a production line in the United States or elsewhere and have unloaded certain materials, equipment and arms on our armed forces which were not really urgently needed at the time, and which could be produced by Canadian manufacturers or could have been replaced after a little while with a better type of material.
I am rather inclined to feel that it is like the man who needs a suit. He cannot get a suit of clothes made by his tailor because his tailor is busy, and he goes to a store and takes an inferior suit off a rack. I should like to issue something of a warning that we do not want any shopworn suits supplied to our forces. When I use the word "suit" I am speaking figuratively, and I am not only referring to uniforms. It must be clearly borne in mind that some of our forces are required for the expansion period. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) referred in his speech to that portion of our armed forces which would provide the manpower for the expanded forces if we should ever enter upon a third world war. I suggest that there is not the same urgency to equip those forces. There is an opportunity for such organizations as Canadian Arsenals Limited to carry out thorough investigation of the type of arm or equipment which will be most desirable, and then to have that put into production in Canada.
I hate to feel that it is possible for a Canadian manufacturer to say: I could have made that if I had known anything about it. Here is a chance to give our Canadian manufacturers the opportunity to build up an industry which will be invaluable to us. See that Canadian Arsenals Limited is working to full capacity, something which I question very much that they are doing at the present time. That is the sort of general advice which I tender in all sincerity to the minister for his consideration.
I want to turn now from the rather broader plane to something which I am afraid you will describe as being of a very local character. I am tempted to make these remarks because I referred a little earlier in the evening to the logging and lumbering industry on Vancouver island. As everybody knows, lumber is a very essential war material. It is urgently required for all kinds of war purposes. As everybody knows, we have a great lumber industry on Vancouver island, but the bottleneck at the present time lies in the ability to ship the lumber off the
[Mr. Pearkes.l

island. It is true there is a shortage of shipping but there is also a shortage of facilities for loading ships at the main ports on Vancouver island.
I have personally seen one vessel loading, another out in the bay and still a third waiting for an opportunity to come in and tie up at the single berth available. If we are going to make the fullest possible use of the amount of lumber that can be produced from our forests, I feel that the question of facilities for loading the very limited number of ships that can be made available for the purpose should be investigated. I know that the larger companies are able to construct their own assembly wharves. Only last week I heard of one company which is building an additional berth at its loading wharf on Vancouver island, but the big companies are operating in the more inaccessible forests of the island leaving many stands of timber to be cut by smaller companies and sent to smaller mills. The small mills have to depend upon the government facilities to get their lumber off the island onto their ships. When it comes to the question of investigating the various means for increasing war industries and making this lumber accessible, may I suggest that this matter be investigated with a view to providing full facilities for the export of the lumber which can be cut in our mills.

Mr. Speaker, since the bill provides
for price controls, I take the liberty of asking the government to establish price controls as soon as possible. We are all aware that the cost of living has reached an astronomical figure and is rising every day.
The government should, I think, establish price controls as soon as possible. Otherwise, the large trusts that control foodstuffs and essential commodities will have time to accumulate large stocks. Then, when the time comes to set basic prices, the trusts holding a monopoly over the purchase, sale and distribution of those products will be in a position to reap tremendous profits.
Immediate action is necessary in order to prevent profiteers from exploiting the people.
There is another point which is of special concern to me; it has to do with statements made recently in the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). He said he intended to return to the system of dollar a year men whom he would choose from the directors of big corporations, monopolies and

industries who control our Canadian economy. That, to my mind, would be a mistake because it would mean putting price control back in the hands of those who are interested in seeing prices rise.
Let me suggest instead the establishment of a price arbitration committee that would include representatives of labour, of the white-collar workers, in short, of people who are completely independent of monopolies.
You know as well as I do that, during the last war, most of the dollar a year men controlling our national economy were directors of large corporations or connected with big concerns. You also know that while they got a dollar a year from the Canadian government, they were still drawing their salary from those companies and necessarily remained interested in the existence and future of their firms.
I feel that this time, in order to satisfy public opinion, when price controls are being considered, we should appoint an arbitration committee to study individual cases, to hear legitimate representations from the various organizations concerned, and then to establish adequate price controls in a serious, independent and competent manner.
Those were the only remarks I wanted to make tonight. I have made them because I feel that it is high time the government took steps to prevent stockpiling and monopolistic profiteering at the expense of the public.
In closing, once again I emphasize the need for prompter government action in setting up price controls in Canada.

I do not know if I am permitted to refer to its wording, Mr. Speaker.

I understand that I may refer to it generally, Mr. Speaker, without going into the specific wording. I presume that is what you intended to convey to me.
By that particular section that I was dealing with, the minister may, if he is satisfied that a person, who has entered into a contract has failed or is even likely to fail-and he determines whether the man is likely to fail-to perform the contract in a businesslike and efficient manner, or if he has failed to keep proper and detailed records-that is, if the minister is satisfied; it is the minister all the way through-he may authorize some person who is named as a controller to go in and take possession of the business and operate it. Then it goes further, Mr. Speaker, and it says, as I understand it, that the controller, if he makes any mistakes, is not to be responsible for them to the owner. In addition, if the owner is required against his will to store materials, even of his own business, and if any of those materials are lost, he himself is responsible for the loss. This is a most extraordinarily worded document.
The final part that I wish to deal with is (this. The act continues until 1956. But the [DOT]governor in council may make ordiers and! regulations to carry out the purposes and provisions of this act. In other words, there is a direct by-pass of parliament all the way through. If this act is to be an act of the parliament of this country under which the people of this country are to have their properties requisitioned, and maybe their persons, that is practically suspending habeas corpus; then the only way that the people of Canada can have the right to protection against the dictatorial powers that the minister will be given under this act is by the insertion in the act of a provision that the minister must report to parliament at regular intervals as to what is happening, and that parliament should have a say in what is happening. I do not mention that point in any idle manner. I mention it in all honesty and all sincerity, so far as I am concerned. It seems to me that no matter how well intentioned a man may be-it is said that power tends to corrupt, and that absolute power corrupts absolutely- it is impossible for any man to have these tremendous powers placed upon his shoulders and not in some way abuse them; that should not be expected. It is beyond a human being's will power not to abuse them. Unconsciously one must do so.
[The Acting Speaker.!
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, not only for the protection of the Canadian people but indeed for the protection of the minister himself, I feel we should have written into this act some provision whereby parliament will have some control of these tremendous powers that the minister will possess under the act.

Mr. Speaker, I have not taken part in the debate on this bill up to this time because I wanted all the time I could possibly get in order to give consideration to its terms and to the principle that is involved in it. I did speak briefly on the resolution which preceded the introduction of the bill, and at that time I think I assured the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) of my good will toward them personally and toward the thing which they had set up to do. I did mention at that time, Mr. Speaker, that I appreciated the democratic way in which the Prime Minister had set about seeking extraordinary powers to clothe the minister with that authority under which he could meet an emergency situation.
I still believe that the Prime Minister was quite right in not proclaiming the War Measures Act. I believe it is far more democratic the way he has set out to do it. But at the same time I do believe, as I suggested when I spoke on the resolution, that it is the wrong principle to ask parliament to clothe a minister and a department with all the powers that may possibly be needed over a long period of time when it is quite possible for parliament to grant sufficient powers at this time to meet the present need, and then at another stage to grant further powers if it is deemed necessary that they be granted.
I suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce once more that I have the highest regard for him personally. What I say tonight I am going to direct to him in the most friendly fashion, with all the good will that I can possibly muster. I think I have made it known to him on numerous occasions that I have no malice whatever toward him; but I do believe that the minister has unnecessarily brought criticism upon himself by asking for too wide powers, not only on this occasion but on former occasions, and I think I have told him across the floor of the house here my feelings on other occasions in that respect.
I wonder what the people of this country would say if they were made fully aware of the powers that the government is asking this parliament to vest in a minister and his deputies and personnel in the new department if parliament were to grant them without question. I can just envision the newspapers across the country saying:	What

kind of opposition have we got down there in parliament? Are those fellows, just on mere suggestion from the government, prepared to shoulder off their responsibilities on to somebody else and to say: Go to it; we do not want any responsibility at all; or are you all down there trying to look after the best interests of the people of this country? I propose that we should, as members of parliament, representing the people, take our responsibilities. We should not try to push them off on the shoulders of somebody else. I propose to be prepared to take my responsibility as a member of this House of Commons in whatever has to be done to meet this situation which has been called a serious emergency situation.
I do not want anybody to feel that I am wishing to shove it off on the minister or the government. Whatever powers are needed to meet the emergency I am prepared to consider handing over to the minister and the government. Anything that is within the competence of this parliament to do to help the government to meet this present situation I think we are bound to do, but I do not think we are bound to do any more than that in this the first stage. I say that, Mr. Speaker, advisedly and I say it for this reason. If any more serious emergency does arise, the government always has an ace in the hole, an ace up its sleeve, in the form of the War Measures Act. They can proclaim it in a moment and deal with a situation that might arise, which is now unforeseen, or for which parliament has not at this stage provided, simply by passing orders in council under the War Measures Act. That is one of the reasons why I feel loath at this time to agree to handing over all of these powers.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) gave this afternoon what I thought was a very complete analysis of the bill and a restrained criticism. At that time he made what I thought were reasonable suggestions. Perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) have already had a chance to consider those suggestions. They may be prepared to bring in some amendments to the bill which will embody what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has requested. But I do think, Mr. Speaker, that, if they have, then it will not hurt to have this bill go over to the first of the week to give them a chance to consider further the request of the opposition and see if they cannot bring in something which will more nearly be acceptable to us all.
I am not ashamed for one second to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am determined it shall go over until the first of the week. I am not
Defence Production Act doing it just for the purpose of being stubborn, or of trying to obstruct. If the matter is as serious as the bill is purported to be, and if the situation in the country is as serious as it is purported to be, then it is serious enough to warrant more than just one day's debate on this matter.
There are a good many things that have occurred to me as a result of the debate that has gone on today that I would like further time to consider in my own mind. Our group has not taken any part in the debate today on second reading for the very reason that we wanted to have just as full information as we could possibly get before we voted on such an important bill as this.
I want to make it abundantly clear to the minister that our position is and has been thus. Whatever powers are needed to meet this present situation he ought to have; but the question in our minds is just how much does he need? That is the principle that is at stake. Should parliament be prepared to give over wide enough powers to meet a hot war in a time when we are not in a hot war, and when everybody in the country is hoping that there will not be a war at all? I do not mean to say that the people of the country are living in any fool's paradise; but let me say that very few people in the country have in their minds anything like a picture of the true situation. I believe that one could sum up their views about this present emergency in the way that a correspondent did for me the other day in a letter when he said something like this. I cannot just remember the exact words, but he did say: I wonder if I shall live long enough to see the start of this war that they have been talking about for so long, and about which a few of us are beginning to plan for? That is just about the way a good many people throughout the country think. They are not prepared. As the minister said in Chicago the other day, and I think he reiterated it here today: You cannot go too far ahead of the people. I think he issued this challenge: Are you prepared to say that labour, the people generally, including all sections of Canada, are prepared to submit to the regimen of over-all controls? He said: Until such time as they are, you cannot make them stick.
That situation applies to the terms of this bill, just the same. What attitude will business take throughout this country? What attitude will industry take, when they see us toiling over the terms of the bill? They will say to themselves: Do those fellows ever give consideration to realities, or are they just prepared to rubber-stamp anything the government puts in front of them, simply because the government may think that an

Defence Production Act emergency situation may develop, and that it will be so intense that they will have to have those powers?
The businessman, the industrialist who is operating a business, will see section 27 and he will naturally ask himself the question- and he will ask us that question when he gets the chance-"Do you fellows actually believe that you have got to force industry and business in this country to do things now? Why do you not try a little inducement, first? Then if we fall down, come in with something that will compel us to do what you want".
Somehow I cannot quite make these two attitudes jibe. It was not many days ago that we were talking in the House of Commons about manpower. I cannot help recalling the fact that a good many spokesmen on the government side said, "Oh, we are not ready for that sort of thing yet. We think we can get more out of the Canadian people, so far as manpower is concerned, by the voluntary method." Now you come along with a bill like this and say, "We are going to compel every businessman and very industrialist in the country to toe the mark that is drawn by the Minister of Trade and Commerce." How do you reconcile those two attitudes? I want to know that.
If we are going to meet an emergency situation we ought to go all-out to meet it.

I do not say that we should be
tender. But let us be consistent

let us be consistent; that is the point. And there is only one way to be consistent, and that is that if we take the position that we can get the best out of people by a process of inducement, we should try some inducement. Then, when that fails, let us go out after the other thing.
I will suggest to the minister this, that he is a master at dealing with men. I am satisfied he knows I am right when I say that if he makes an appeal to the industrialists and businessmen of this country for certain things he will just about get one hundred per cent of what he asks for, without compelling them. I do not think there would be any question about it-and I think also that I am paying the minister a high compliment when I say that.
I believe that without going into detail- and I have many of them before me which I have not time to discuss this evening-I should suggest that both of the ministers who are here this evening, listening, in the last minutes of this day, should take into


consideration what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked earlier today.
Let me review what he asked, for the benefit of the house. I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) did agree provision should be made for an annual report. That is good. But I believe also that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was making a most reasonable request when he asked, "Do you not think you had better reconsider the time limit?" If the defence program is designed to cover a period of three years, then why make provision in this measure for five years, almost double the time you expect your defence program to cover?
I have not heard anything in the debate thus far to change my mind on that matter. I thin-k we should relate the two in some way, and not ask that these provisions cover too long a time.
He made the further suggestion that consideration be given to dividing the powers in this field, by setting up a list of those the minister needs right now, and which he could now justify, alongside another group which could be proclaimed when the need arose, and the powers with respect to which could be taken by the minister to meet whatever emergency he might have to meet at that time.
That would at least recognize the principle I have already suggested, and that is that we would try to dio as much as we possibly can by the principle of inducement, and to leave compulsion for the time being, until it has to be used. I would not be prepared to write that list, because I know it would be difficult. I am not even sure that it could be written. However, it certainly is a suggestion that could be studied over the week end. Perhaps the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be able to make some suggestion at the first of next week to set our minds at rest in that respect.
I am in agreement with the main principle of the bill. I believe the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is also in agreement with it-in fact everyone who spoke today probably was. But we did make reservations when we spoke on the resolution stage, and one of those reservations was: Let us not go beyond what we need now. Parliament will be in session for months to come and can be called back quickly, in case of emergency. When we need to give the minister further powers, let us give them to him. Let me say once again, in a friendly way, to the Minister of Trade and1 Commerce; for goodness' sake

do not give these fellows ammunition to throw back at you, and to claim that you are a dictator.
